messages.content: Lesson 1: What is a vector?

Direction + magnitude. In 3D: (x, y, z). Not a position — a displacement. Adding vector to a point gives another point. Two points subtracted give a vector. Length: sqrt(x²+y²+z²). Unit vector: length = 1, pure direction.
Lesson 2: Vector addition and subtraction

Add: (a.x+b.x, a.y+b.y, a.z+b.z). Chain of displacements. Commutative: a+b = b+a.
Subtract: a-b = vector FROM b TO a. Not commutative. To get direction from A to B: B-A, then normalize.
Lesson 3: Vector magnitude and normalization

Magnitude: |v| = sqrt(x²+y²+z²). Expensive — sqrt. If you only need to compare distances, compare squared magnitudes instead: x²+y²+z² — no sqrt.
Normalize: v/|v|. Unit vector. Always check magnitude > 0 first or you divide by zero → NaN.
Lesson 4: Scalar multiplication

v * s = (x*s, y*s, z*s). Scales magnitude, preserves direction. Negative scalar reverses direction.
Use: speed * direction = velocity. Normalize direction first, then scale by speed. Never scale a non-unit vector by speed — you'll get magnitude × speed.
Lesson 5: Distance between two points

(B-A).Length(). That's it. But sqrt is expensive — if comparing distances, use (B-A).LengthSquared() and compare against threshold². Same result, no sqrt. This matters in loops over thousands of entities.
Lesson 6: Dot product

a·b = ax*bx + ay*by + az*bz. Scalar. Measures alignment.
Unit vectors: a·b = cos(angle). +1 same, 0 perpendicular, -1 opposite.
Three multiplies, two adds. No sqrt, no trig. The cheapest geometric test.
Lesson 7: Dot product for facing
dot(npcForward, normalize(target - npc.position)). Positive = target in front. Negative = behind. Zero = exactly to the side. Cheaper than computing the actual angle.
Lesson 8: Dot product for vision cones

dot(forward, toTarget) > cos(halfAngle). If true, target is inside the cone.
Store cos(halfAngle) as a constant — never compute acos at runtime just to compare.
Fish.h: GetVisionCosAngle() returns 0.5 = cos(60°) = 120° cone.
Lesson 9: Dot product for projection

Project v onto axis: dot(v, normalize(axis)) gives the signed length of v along axis.
Project v onto plane with normal n: v - n * dot(v, n). Subtracts the normal component.
Used for: shadow lengths, distance along a ray, terrain slope measurement.
Lesson 10: Dot product for lighting

Lambert diffuse: intensity = max(0, dot(surfaceNormal, lightDir)). Surface facing light = bright, facing away = dark, perpendicular = zero.
This is why normals matter — wrong normal = wrong lighting. Per-vertex or per-pixel normals change the quality.
Lesson 11: Cross product

a×b = (ay*bz-az*by, az*bx-ax*bz, ax*by-ay*bx). Vector perpendicular to both.
|a×b| = |a||b|sin(angle). Right-hand rule for direction.
Not commutative: a×b = -(b×a). Parallel vectors give zero.
Lesson 12: Cross product for normals

Surface normal = normalize(cross(edge1, edge2)). edge1 = v1-v0, edge2 = v2-v0.
Winding order matters — swap edges and normal flips. CW vs CCW convention.
Degenerate triangles (collinear verts) give zero cross — check before normalizing.
Lesson 13: Cross product for rotation axis

axis = normalize(cross(from, to)). Angle = acos(dot(from, to)).
This is exactly what Quaternion::FromRotationTo does internally.
Edge case: parallel vectors give zero cross — no unique rotation axis. Check dot ≈ ±1.
Lesson 14: Cross product for winding order

2D: cross(edge1, edge2).z > 0 = CCW, < 0 = CW. Determines front vs back face.
3D: dot(cross(edge1, edge2), viewDir) < 0 = facing away = backface cull.
GPU does this per-triangle automatically, but you need it for procedural mesh generation.
Lesson 15: Dot and cross together

atan2(|cross(a,b)|, dot(a,b)) = full signed angle. Better than acos(dot) alone.
Dot = cosine (how much alignment). Cross = sine and axis (which direction).
Together: complete relative orientation decomposed into axis + angle.
Lesson 16: What is a matrix?

Grid of numbers that transforms vectors. 3x3 = rotation+scale. 4x4 = rotation+scale+translation.
Multiply matrix × vector = transformed vector. Multiply matrix × matrix = combined transform.
Identity matrix: no change. Inverse: undoes the transform. Transpose: rows↔columns.
Lesson 17: Matrix multiplication

A × B ≠ B × A. Order matters — transforms apply right to left.
M = Translation × Rotation × Scale means: scale first, then rotate, then translate.
In Urho3D: Matrix3x4 combines rotation+scale+translation. Node::GetWorldTransform() returns this.
Lesson 18: Transform hierarchy

Child's world transform = parent's world transform × child's local transform.
Move parent → children follow. Rotate parent → children orbit.
Node::GetWorldPosition() walks up the hierarchy. SetPosition() is local to parent.
This is the scene graph — the most important data structure in a game engine.
Lesson 19: Inverse transform

World to local: multiply by inverse of the world transform.
Use: convert a world-space click position into an object's local space for hit testing.
Urho3D: node->GetWorldTransform().Inverse() × worldPoint = localPoint.
For pure rotation: inverse = transpose. Cheaper than general inverse.
Lesson 20: What is a quaternion?

4D number (w, x, y, z) representing a 3D rotation. No gimbal lock unlike Euler angles.
Unit quaternion: w²+x²+y²+z² = 1. Multiply two quaternions = combine rotations.
From axis+angle: Quaternion(angle, axis). From Euler: Quaternion(pitch, yaw, roll).
Urho3D default: Quaternion::IDENTITY = no rotation.
Lesson 21: Why quaternions over Euler angles?

Euler: pitch, yaw, roll — intuitive but broken. Gimbal lock at ±90° pitch. Interpolation is ugly.
Quaternion: no gimbal lock, smooth interpolation (slerp), compact (4 floats), fast composition.
Rule: store rotations as quaternions. Convert to Euler only for UI display. Never accumulate Euler angles.
Lesson 22: Quaternion slerp

Slerp(a, b, t): spherical linear interpolation. t=0 gives a, t=1 gives b, 0.5 gives halfway rotation.
Smooth, constant-speed rotation along the shortest arc. Used for animation blending, camera smoothing.
Urho3D: a.Slerp(b, t). Handles the shortest-path check automatically.
Lesson 23: Quaternion from rotation to

Quaternion::FromRotationTo(from, to): rotation that transforms direction 'from' into direction 'to'.
Internally: axis = cross(from, to), angle = acos(dot(from, to)).
Used in AssetTool AutoFace Z+: rotate model so hip-to-neck axis faces forward.
Lesson 24: Quaternion multiplication

q1 * q2 = combined rotation. Apply q2 first, then q1.
Not commutative: q1*q2 ≠ q2*q1. Rotating around X then Y ≠ Y then X.
To rotate a vector: q * Vector3 uses Urho3D's operator*. Internally: q × v × q⁻¹.
Lesson 25: Euler angles

Pitch (X), Yaw (Y), Roll (Z). Intuitive for humans, dangerous for code.
Gimbal lock: at pitch ±90°, yaw and roll become the same axis — lose a degree of freedom.
Urho3D uses degrees: Quaternion(pitch, yaw, roll). GetEulerAngles() to extract.
Use for: UI sliders, debug display. Never for runtime rotation accumulation.
Lesson 26: Linear interpolation (lerp)

Lerp(a, b, t) = a + (b-a)*t. t=0→a, t=1→b, t=0.5→midpoint.
Works for floats, vectors, colors. Fast — one multiply, one add.
For positions: smooth movement. For colors: fade transitions.
Urho3D: Lerp(a, b, t) in MathDefs.h.
Lesson 27: Smoothstep

Smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) = smooth S-curve between 0 and 1.
Unlike lerp: starts slow, accelerates, decelerates, arrives slow. Natural-looking.
Formula: t = clamp((x-edge0)/(edge1-edge0), 0, 1); return t*t*(3-2*t).
Use for: fade-in/out, terrain blending, smooth thresholds.
Lesson 28: Clamping

Clamp(value, min, max). Keeps value within bounds.
Essential for: HP (0 to maxHP), fuel ratio (0 to 1), audio gain (0 to 1), UI positions.
Urho3D: Clamp(v, lo, hi) in MathDefs.h. Also Min(a,b) and Max(a,b).
Lesson 29: Trigonometry basics

sin(angle) = opposite/hypotenuse. cos(angle) = adjacent/hypotenuse.
Unit circle: (cos θ, sin θ) traces a circle. Used for circular motion, wave effects.
atan2(y, x) = angle from positive X axis. Handles all quadrants — better than atan(y/x).
Urho3D uses degrees in most APIs. C++ math uses radians. Convert: rad = deg * M_DEGTORAD.
Lesson 30: Why atan2 not atan

atan(y/x): loses quadrant info (can't tell +x from -x). Division by zero when x=0.
atan2(y, x): full -π to π range, handles all quadrants, no division by zero.
Use: heading from position delta. float angle = atan2(dz, dx). Always atan2, never atan.
Lesson 31: Coordinate systems

Urho3D: Y-up, right-handed. +X = right, +Y = up, +Z = forward (into screen).
Screen: (0,0) = top-left, +X right, +Y down.
UV: (0,0) = top-left of texture, (1,1) = bottom-right.
World vs local: world = absolute, local = relative to parent node.
Lesson 32: World vs local space

Local: relative to parent. SetPosition(0,1,0) = 1 unit above parent.
World: absolute. GetWorldPosition() = position in scene coordinates.
Convert local→world: parent.GetWorldTransform() × localPos.
Convert world→local: parent.GetWorldTransform().Inverse() × worldPos.
Lesson 33: Perlin noise

Smooth random values that vary continuously — no sudden jumps.
Input: position (1D, 2D, or 3D). Output: value typically -1 to 1.
Octaves: layer multiple frequencies. Low frequency = broad hills, high = fine detail.
Used in: terrain generation, cloud shapes, wind variation, water ripples.
TerrainGenerator uses it with ridged multifractal for mountain ridges.
Lesson 34: Random numbers in games

SetRandomSeed(seed): deterministic sequence. Same seed = same results. Essential for replays/networking.
Random() = 0.0-1.0 float. Random(min, max) = range.
Random(intMax) = 0 to intMax-1.
Never use rand() from C stdlib — not thread-safe, bad distribution. Use engine's Random().
Lesson 35: Bezier curves

Control points define a smooth curve. Quadratic: 3 points. Cubic: 4 points.
Evaluate at t (0-1): nested lerps. Cubic: lerp(lerp(lerp(p0,p1,t), lerp(p1,p2,t), t), lerp(lerp(p1,p2,t), lerp(p2,p3,t), t), t).
Use for: camera paths, animation curves, UI transitions, DrivenKey smooth mode.
Lesson 36: Catmull-Rom splines

Passes through all control points (unlike Bezier which only passes through endpoints).
4 points needed per segment: previous, start, end, next.
Used in DrivenKeySystem: mode 'catmullrom' interpolates through all defined points.
Good for: path following, animation curves where you want exact waypoint hits.
Lesson 37: Frustum culling

Camera sees a truncated pyramid (frustum). Objects outside = don't render.
6 planes: near, far, left, right, top, bottom. Test object's bounding box against all 6.
If fully outside any plane = culled. Urho3D does this automatically per drawable.
Octree accelerates this — spatial subdivision means most objects aren't even tested.
Lesson 38: Bounding volumes

AABB: axis-aligned bounding box. Fast intersection test but rotates badly (gets loose).
OBB: oriented bounding box. Tighter but more expensive to test.
Sphere: cheapest test (distance < radius), worst fit for elongated objects.
Urho3D uses AABB for octree and frustum culling. BoundingBox class: min_ and max_ corners.
Lesson 39: Rays and raycasting

Ray: origin + direction. Point on ray: origin + direction * t (t ≥ 0).
Raycast: shoot ray into scene, find first intersection. Returns position, normal, distance, drawable.
Urho3D: octree->RaycastSingle(ray, result, maxDist) for rendering hits.
Physics: physicsWorld->RaycastSingle(ray, maxDist, result) for collision hits.
Used for: mouse picking, line of sight, ground detection, bullet traces.
Lesson 40: Terrain height sampling

terrain->GetHeight(Vector3(x, 0, z)). Returns Y at that XZ position.
Interpolates between heightmap pixels — smooth result.
Used everywhere: placing objects, gravity, slope checks, water depth.
Cheap operation — just a texture lookup + bilinear interpolation.
Lesson 41: What is a pointer?

Address of something in memory. int* p = &x; *p reads/writes x through the address.
Null pointer = points to nothing. Dereferencing null = crash (segfault).
Always check: if (ptr) before using. Or use references when null isn't valid.
Lesson 42: Stack vs heap

Stack: automatic, fast, scoped. int x = 5; — dies at end of scope. Fixed size.
Heap: manual, slower, persistent. new/delete. Lives until you free it.
Stack overflow: too many nested calls or huge local arrays.
Rule: prefer stack. Use heap only for objects that outlive the scope or are too large.
Lesson 43: RAII

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. Constructor acquires, destructor releases.
File: open in constructor, close in destructor. Lock: acquire in constructor, release in destructor.
No manual cleanup needed — scope exit triggers destructor automatically.
Urho3D SharedPtr/WeakPtr are RAII for reference-counted objects.
Lesson 44: Smart pointers

SharedPtr<T>: reference counted. Object deleted when last SharedPtr dies. Urho3D's primary ownership.
WeakPtr<T>: doesn't keep object alive. Check Expired() or Get() before use. Safe observer.
UniquePtr: sole owner, not copyable, movable. Not used much in Urho3D.
Never mix raw new with SharedPtr — use MakeShared or constructor.
Lesson 45: References vs pointers

Reference: alias, never null, can't reseat. int& r = x; r is x.
Pointer: can be null, can point to different things. More flexible, more dangerous.
Const reference: const T& — read-only, no copy. Use for function parameters.
Rule: use references when null is never valid. Use pointers when null is meaningful (optional).
Lesson 46: Const correctness

const int x = 5; — can't modify x.
const T& param — function won't modify the argument.
Method() const — method doesn't modify the object. Required for const references.
const T* vs T* const: first = pointer to const data, second = const pointer to mutable data.
Rule: make everything const unless it needs to be mutable. Compiler catches bugs for you.
Lesson 47: Virtual functions

virtual: method can be overridden in derived class. Resolved at runtime via vtable.
override: compiler verifies you're actually overriding something (catches typos).
Pure virtual: = 0. Makes the class abstract — can't instantiate.
Urho3D: Component::Update is virtual. Override in your LogicComponent subclass.
Lesson 48: Inheritance

class Dog : public Animal. Dog IS-A Animal. Dog inherits Animal's methods and data.
Public inheritance: base's public stays public. Protected stays protected.
Prefer composition over deep inheritance. 2-3 levels max.
Urho3D: Object → Serializable → Animatable → Component → LogicComponent → YourClass.
Lesson 49: Move semantics

Move: transfer ownership instead of copying. String a = std::move(b); — b is now empty, a has b's data.
Move constructor: T(T&& other). Move assignment: T& operator=(T&& other).
Use for: returning large objects from functions, container insertion.
Avoids expensive copies. The compiler does this automatically in many cases (return value optimization).
Lesson 50: Templates

Generic code. template<typename T> T Max(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }
Compiler generates a new function for each type used: Max<int>, Max<float>.
Urho3D: SharedPtr<T>, WeakPtr<T>, Vector<T>, HashMap<K,V> are all templates.
Keep templates in headers — compiler needs the full definition at each use site.
Lesson 51: Hash maps

Key→Value lookup in O(1) average. Urho3D: HashMap<K,V>.
Insert: map[key] = value. Find: auto it = map.Find(key); if (it != map.End()) use it->second_.
Good for: entity lookups by ID, caching, spatial hashing.
Bad for: ordered iteration, cache coherency (scattered memory).
Lesson 52: Vectors (containers)

Dynamic array. Urho3D: Vector<T>. Contiguous memory — cache friendly.
Push: vec.Push(item). Access: vec[i]. Size: vec.Size(). Remove: vec.Erase(i).
Reserve: vec.Reserve(n) — preallocate to avoid reallocation.
Iterate: for (unsigned i = 0; i < vec.Size(); ++i) or range-for.
Bad for: frequent insert/remove in the middle (shifts all elements).
Lesson 53: Strings

Urho3D: String class. Not std::string.
Construct: String s("hello"). Concatenate: s + " world" or s.Append(other).
Compare: s == other, s.Contains("sub"), s.StartsWith("pre").
Format: String::Format("%d items", count) — but URHO3D_LOGINFOF is preferred for logging.
Empty check: s.Empty(), not s.Length() == 0.
Lesson 54: Spatial hashing

Divide world into grid cells. Each entity goes in the cell its position maps to.
Neighbor query: check only the 9 (2D) or 27 (3D) surrounding cells.
O(1) lookup vs O(n) brute force. Massive speedup for proximity queries.
Used in codebase: FishSpatialHash for nearby fish, LandAnimalSpatialHash for creature queries.
Lesson 55: State machines

Entity has a current state. Each state defines behavior and transitions.
NPC AI: IDLE→HUNT→ATTACK→FLEE. Only one state active.
Implement: enum + switch in update. Or: virtual State with Enter/Update/Exit.
Urho3D NPCs: ai.state is an int, switch in TickCreatureAI.
Keep states simple. Complex behavior = more states, not bigger states.
Lesson 56: Game loop

while(running) { ProcessInput(); Update(dt); Render(); }
dt = delta time since last frame. Multiply all movement/timers by dt for frame-rate independence.
Fixed timestep for physics (deterministic). Variable timestep for rendering (smooth).
Urho3D: Engine::RunFrame() does input→update→render. Subscribe to E_UPDATE for your logic.
Lesson 57: Component system

Entity = Node. Behavior = Component. Attach components to nodes.
Better than deep inheritance: Node + StaticModel + RigidBody + MyScript vs class PhysicsMeshEntity.
Components are independent — add/remove at runtime. Mix and match.
Urho3D: node->CreateComponent<T>(). GetComponent<T>(). Component::Update() called per frame.
Lesson 58: Event-driven architecture

Instead of polling: subscribe to events, get called when things happen.
Decouples sender from receiver. Button doesn't know who handles the click.
Urho3D: SubscribeToEvent(E_RELEASED, handler). SendEvent(E_MYEVENT, data).
VariantMap carries event data — type-safe key-value pairs.
Avoid event storms — don't send events every frame if polling would be cheaper.
Lesson 59: Scene graphs

Tree of nodes. Each node has transform relative to parent. Children inherit parent's transform.
Move a vehicle node → wheels, seats, passengers all move with it.
Urho3D: Scene is the root. CreateChild() builds the tree. GetChild(name, recursive) searches it.
Performance: deep trees are fine. Wide trees (1000 children on one node) get slow for traversal.
Lesson 60: Resource management

Load once, use many. ResourceCache returns the same object for the same path.
100 NPCs share one Model object. Clone Materials only when you need different parameters.
Never load the same resource twice manually. Always go through ResourceCache.
Urho3D: GetSubsystem<ResourceCache>()->GetResource<T>(path).
Lesson 61: Rendering pipeline overview

Application → Scene → Octree culling → Batch collection → Sort → GPU draw.
1. Frustum cull: reject invisible objects
2. Collect batches: group by material/geometry for efficiency
3. Sort: opaque front-to-back (early-Z), transparent back-to-front (blending)
4. Submit draw calls to GPU
5. Post-processing passes (blur, bloom, god rays)
Lesson 62: What is a shader?

Small program that runs on GPU. Vertex shader: transforms vertices. Fragment shader: computes pixel color.
Inputs: attributes (position, normal, UV), uniforms (camera matrix, light direction, time).
Output: vertex shader → clip-space position. Fragment shader → pixel color.
GLSL: C-like language. vec3, mat4, texture(), mix(), clamp().
Lesson 63: Vertex shaders

Runs once per vertex. Job: transform position from model space to clip space.
Minimum: gl_Position = projectionMatrix * viewMatrix * modelMatrix * vec4(position, 1.0).
Also: pass UV, normal, color to fragment shader via varyings.
Can deform geometry: grass waving, water waves, skeletal animation on GPU.
Lesson 64: Fragment shaders

Runs once per pixel (fragment). Job: compute final color.
Inputs: interpolated varyings from vertex shader (UV, normal, worldPos).
Texture sampling: texture(diffMap, uv). Lighting: dot(normal, lightDir). Fog: mix with fog color.
Output: gl_FragColor or output variable. Alpha < 1 = transparent (needs alpha blending).
Lesson 65: Textures

2D image mapped onto 3D geometry via UV coordinates.
UV: (0,0) to (1,1). Values outside wrap (repeat) or clamp depending on addressing mode.
Filtering: nearest (pixelated), bilinear (smooth), trilinear (smooth + mipmap), anisotropic (sharp at angles).
Mipmaps: pre-scaled copies. GPU picks appropriate level by distance. Avoids aliasing.
Lesson 66: Materials

Package of: technique + textures + parameters.
Technique: which shaders and render passes to use.
Textures: diffuse (color), normal (bumps), specular (shininess), emissive (glow).
Parameters: MatDiffColor, MatSpecColor — set via XML or runtime SetShaderParameter().
Urho3D: Material XML files in bin/Data/Materials/. Clone() for per-instance variants.
Lesson 67: Lighting models

Ambient: constant minimum light everywhere. Fakes indirect illumination.
Diffuse (Lambert): dot(normal, lightDir). Matte surfaces.
Specular (Blinn-Phong): dot(normal, halfVector)^shininess. Shiny highlights.
Emissive: self-illumination. Doesn't light other objects.
PBR: physically-based. Metallic + roughness replace diffuse + specular. More realistic.
Lesson 68: Forward vs deferred rendering

Forward: each object rendered once per light. Simple but expensive with many lights.
Deferred: geometry pass writes to G-Buffer (position, normal, albedo). Lighting pass reads G-Buffer.
Deferred handles many lights cheaply. Cost = geometry pass + one pass per light on a quad.
Downside: no MSAA on G-Buffer (expensive), transparent objects need forward fallback.
Urho3D: supports both. RenderPaths/Forward.xml or RenderPaths/Deferred.xml.
Lesson 69: Client-server architecture

Server: authoritative. Owns all game state. Validates everything.
Client: predicts locally for responsiveness. Server corrects if wrong.
Never trust the client — it can be modified. All important logic server-side.
Urho3D: built-in replication. REPLICATED nodes sync automatically. LOCAL nodes are client-only.
Lesson 70: Network replication

Server creates REPLICATED nodes → automatically appear on clients.
Delta updates: only changed attributes sent. Bandwidth efficient.
Node Vars: SetVar(hash, value) on replicated node → syncs to all clients.
Custom messages: connection->SendMessage(id, reliable, ordered, buffer) for game-specific data.
Registered remote events: network->RegisterRemoteEvent(hash) for event-based sync.
Lesson 71: Protocol design

Message = ID + payload. ID is a byte or short. Payload is packed binary.
Pack with VectorBuffer: buf.WriteU16(count), buf.WriteFloat(x), buf.WriteString(name).
Unpack with MemoryBuffer: msg.ReadU16(), msg.ReadFloat(), msg.ReadString().
Keep messages small. Send deltas, not full state. Batch where possible.
Lesson 72: Latency and prediction

Network delay = 20-200ms. Player sees stale state.
Client prediction: apply input locally, don't wait for server. Feels responsive.
Server reconciliation: if server disagrees, snap or lerp to corrected position.
Interpolation: buffer server updates, play back slightly delayed for smooth motion.
Urho3D: client prediction via serverDriven_ flag in HumanNPC.
Lesson 73: Collision detection basics

Broad phase: cheap test to reject far-apart objects (AABB overlap, spatial hash).
Narrow phase: precise test on candidates (GJK, SAT, mesh intersection).
Bullet physics handles both automatically when you add RigidBody + CollisionShape.
For custom checks: distance < sumOfRadii (sphere), AABB overlap test, raycast.
Lesson 74: Rigid body dynamics

Mass > 0 = dynamic (affected by forces). Mass = 0 = static (immovable).
Forces: ApplyForce (continuous), ApplyImpulse (instant). Gravity applied automatically.
Friction and restitution (bounciness) control surface interaction.
Urho3D: node->CreateComponent<RigidBody>(), SetMass(1.0f), SetFriction(0.5f).
Lesson 75: Raycasting for gameplay

Mouse pick: camera->GetScreenRay(mouseX/screenW, mouseY/screenH). Cast into scene.
Ground check: ray from entity downward, find terrain hit.
Line of sight: ray from NPC to target, check if anything blocks.
Bullet trace: ray along aim direction, first hit = damage target.
Always set maxDistance — infinite rays are expensive.
Lesson 76: 3D audio

SoundSource3D: positioned in world. Volume attenuates with distance from listener.
SoundListener: on camera node. Only one active listener.
Near/far distance: full volume within near, silence beyond far. Linear fallback between.
Urho3D: node->CreateComponent<SoundSource3D>(). audio->SetListener(listenerComponent).
Lesson 77: Audio mixing

Multiple sounds play simultaneously. Engine mixes them.
Gain: per-source volume (0-1). Master gain: per-category (SOUND_EFFECT, SOUND_MUSIC, SOUND_AMBIENT).
Priority: when too many sources, lowest priority gets dropped.
Looping: sound->SetLooped(true). One-shot: play and forget (REMOVE_COMPONENT on finish).
Lesson 78: UI layout

Absolute: SetPosition(x, y), SetSize(w, h). Pixel-perfect but doesn't scale.
Anchors: SetMinAnchor(0,0), SetMaxAnchor(1,1). Normalized coords — scales with window.
Layout modes: LM_FREE (manual), LM_HORIZONTAL, LM_VERTICAL. Auto-arrange children.
Combine: anchors for panels, layout modes for content within panels.
Lesson 79: UI events

E_RELEASED: button clicked. E_TEXTFINISHED: enter pressed in LineEdit.
E_ITEMSELECTED: dropdown/list selection changed. E_SLIDERCHANGED: slider moved.
E_TOGGLED: checkbox state changed. E_HOVERBEGIN/E_HOVEREND: mouse enter/leave.
Subscribe to specific sender: SubscribeToEvent(button, E_RELEASED, handler).
Event data: P_ELEMENT gives the source UIElement.
Lesson 80: SQLite basics

Embedded database — no server, just a file. Perfect for game data.
Prepare: sqlite3_prepare_v2(db, sql, -1, &stmt, nullptr).
Bind: sqlite3_bind_int(stmt, 1, value). NEVER concatenate strings into SQL.
Step: sqlite3_step(stmt). SQLITE_ROW = has data, SQLITE_DONE = finished.
Read: sqlite3_column_int(stmt, 0), sqlite3_column_text(stmt, 1).
Finalize: sqlite3_finalize(stmt). Always.
Lesson 81: SQL injection

NEVER: String sql = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE name = '" + userInput + "'";
Attacker inputs: ' OR 1=1 -- and gets all rows. Or worse: '; DROP TABLE items; --
ALWAYS: parameterized queries. sqlite3_prepare_v2 with ? placeholders + sqlite3_bind_*.
Every SQL query in this codebase must use parameterized binding. No exceptions.
Lesson 82: Threading basics

Thread: independent execution path. Multiple threads = concurrent work.
Mutex: lock before accessing shared data. std::mutex + std::lock_guard.
Deadlock: thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1.
Rule: lock for the shortest possible time. Never hold two locks simultaneously if avoidable.
Urho3D: WorkQueue for parallel jobs. Never modify scene from worker threads.
Lesson 83: File locking

flock(fd, LOCK_EX): exclusive lock — one holder at a time. LOCK_SH: shared (readers).
LOCK_NB: non-blocking — fail immediately if can't lock.
O_CLOEXEC: close fd on exec — prevents lock leaking to child processes.
flock is per-open-file-description. Two fds to same file = two independent locks.
This codebase uses flock for build safety, workboard access, and singleton guards.
Lesson 84: Process management

PID: unique process identifier. /proc/<pid>/ exists while process is alive.
test -d /proc/<pid> is the ONLY reliable liveness check. ps can give false negatives.
kill(pid, 0): check if process exists without sending a signal.
fork(): create child process. Child inherits open file descriptors — beware lock leakage.
Lesson 85: Debugging with print

URHO3D_LOGINFO("message") — info level.
URHO3D_LOGWARNING("warning") — something odd.
URHO3D_LOGERROR("error") — something broke.
URHO3D_LOGINFOF("value: %d", x) — formatted. Printf-style.
Log goes to <AppName>.log in the working directory.
Never leave debug spam in shipped code. Use #ifdef URHO3D_LOGGING or remove.
Lesson 86: Assertions

assert(condition): crash immediately if false. Debug-only — stripped in release.
Use for: conditions that should NEVER be false. Null pointers that can't be null. Array bounds.
Don't use for: user input validation, network data, file existence. Those can legitimately fail.
ggml uses GGML_ABORT for assertion failures — that's what crashes Yuki when tensors go wrong.
Lesson 87: Memory alignment

CPU reads memory in aligned chunks (4, 8, 16 bytes). Misaligned access is slow or crashes.
Struct padding: compiler inserts gaps to align members. sizeof(struct) ≥ sum of member sizes.
SIMD (SSE/AVX) requires 16/32-byte alignment. alignas(16) in C++.
GPU uniform buffers require std140 layout — specific alignment rules per type.
Lesson 88: Cache coherency

CPU cache: fast memory near the processor. Cache line = 64 bytes.
Contiguous data (arrays, Vector<T>) = cache friendly. Fast.
Scattered data (linked lists, HashMap) = cache misses. Slow.
Iterate arrays linearly when possible. Structure of arrays > array of structures for hot loops.
This is why spatial hashing uses a grid — nearby queries hit nearby memory.
Lesson 89: Profiling

Measure first, optimize second. Never guess at bottlenecks.
ProfilerUI: GPU/CPU timing overlay in all samples. Shows frame time breakdown.
ProfilerTimeline: Chrome trace export for detailed analysis.
RenderDoc: GPU frame capture — see every draw call, texture, shader.
Rule: if you can't measure the improvement, you didn't make one.
Lesson 90: Object pooling

Allocating/freeing objects is expensive. Pool: pre-allocate, reuse.
Activate: grab from pool, initialize. Deactivate: reset, return to pool.
Used for: bullets, particles, NPC AI states, network buffers.
Urho3D: VulkanConstantBufferPool for GPU memory. ParticleEmitter reuses particle slots.
Lesson 91: Delta time

Time since last frame. E_UPDATE gives P_TIMESTEP.
Multiply all per-frame changes by dt: position += velocity * dt.
Without dt: game runs 2x fast at 120fps vs 60fps. With dt: consistent regardless of framerate.
Accumulate timers: timer += dt. Fire when timer >= interval. Reset: timer -= interval (not = 0).
Lesson 92: Fixed vs variable timestep

Variable: dt varies per frame. Smooth rendering but physics can be inconsistent.
Fixed: constant dt (e.g. 1/60s). Accumulate real time, step physics in fixed increments.
Urho3D physics uses fixed timestep internally. Your E_UPDATE gets variable dt.
For gameplay timers: use real dt. For physics: let Bullet handle it.
Lesson 93: Particle systems

Many small billboards simulating fire, smoke, sparks, rain.
ParticleEffect: emission rate, lifetime, velocity, color over time, size over time.
ParticleEmitter: component that spawns particles from an effect.
ColorFrames: color changes over particle lifetime. SetNumColorFrames + SetColorFrame.
Urho3D: cache->GetResource<ParticleEffect>("Particle/Fire.xml"). Clone() for variants.
Lesson 94: Animation blending

Multiple animations on one skeleton. Each has a weight (0-1) and layer.
Layer 0: base (walk/run). Layer 1: upper body overlay (attack while walking).
Weights on same layer blend proportionally. Higher layer overrides lower.
Urho3D: AnimationState::SetWeight(0.5f), SetLayer(1). CrossFade by ramping weights.
Lesson 95: Skeletal animation

Skeleton: hierarchy of bones. Each bone has local transform relative to parent.
Animation: keyframes — bone transforms at specific times. Engine interpolates between.
Bind pose: the default pose the mesh was modeled in. Animations are deltas from bind.
Skinning: each vertex influenced by 1-4 bones with weights. GPU does the blending.
Lesson 96: Animation text keys

Markers at specific frames in an animation. Fire events when reached during playback.
E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY: handler receives the key name/data at the right moment.
Use for: footstep sounds at foot-down frame, weapon attach at grab frame, particle spawn at impact.
Urho3D: .json sidecar next to .ani file defines text keys. Auto-loaded.
This is the event channel — animation files become timestamped event timelines.
Lesson 97: L-systems

String rewriting rules that generate fractal structures. Axiom → apply rules → interpret.
F = draw forward. + = turn right. - = turn left. [ = push state. ] = pop state.
Iterations increase complexity: 'F' → 'F[+F][-F]' → 'F[+F][-F][+F[+F][-F]][-F[+F][-F]]'.
Used in: LTreeGenerator for procedural trees. Also works for: rivers, roots, road networks.
FishingRod: axiom 'FFFFF', no branching rules = straight tapered stick.
Lesson 98: Octrees

3D space divided into 8 children recursively. Each node holds objects within its bounds.
Query: traverse only branches that overlap the query volume. Skip entire subtrees.
Used for: frustum culling, raycast acceleration, proximity queries.
Urho3D: Octree component on Scene. All Drawables auto-insert. octree->Raycast() uses it.
Lesson 99: LOD (Level of Detail)

Far objects use simpler meshes. Save GPU work without visible quality loss.
Discrete LOD: 2-3 mesh versions, swap by distance.
Continuous LOD: mesh simplification based on distance.
Urho3D: StaticModel supports multiple LOD levels in one Model. Auto-selects by distance.
Trees: LTreeGenerator::GenerateLOD() makes fewer-iteration versions for distance.
Lesson 100: Billboards

Flat quad that always faces the camera. Cheap impostor for distant objects.
Used for: particles, distant trees, lens flares, moon, sun.
Urho3D: BillboardSet component. Efficient — one draw call for all billboards in a set.
Camera-facing: rotate to match view direction each frame. Or axis-constrained (Y-up only).
